---
title: "The brain region hierarchy"
---

Brain regions in `iblatlas` are not a flat list. They form a tree, and a region can be referred
to by three different identifiers that are easy to mistake for one another. Both facts cause
confusion often enough to be worth stating plainly.

## Regions form a tree

Every region has a parent, up to the root. `BrainRegions` holds the whole structure tree, and
`ancestors` walks it:

```python
from iblatlas.regions import BrainRegions

br = BrainRegions()
br.ancestors(985).acronym
# array(['root', 'grey', 'CH', 'CTX', 'CTXpl', 'Isocortex', 'MO', 'MOp'], ...)
```

Primary motor area sits eight levels down, inside `MO`, inside `Isocortex`, and so on up to
`root`. Depth is recorded in `br.level`, which runs 0 to 10.

This is what makes granularity adjustable. A recording assigned to `MOp` is also, truthfully,
in `Isocortex` and in `grey`. Choosing how coarsely to describe it is choosing a level of the
tree — which is what the [mappings](brain-region-mappings.qmd) do systematically.

## Three identifiers, and they are not interchangeable

| Identifier | Example for primary motor area | What it is | Stable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Acronym** | `MOp` | Short human-readable label | Yes |
| **Allen id** | `985` | The Allen Institute's region id | Yes |
| **Index** | `19` | Row number in this `BrainRegions` object | **No** |

The acronym and the Allen id are properties of the region and stay put. The **index** is a
position in the arrays `BrainRegions` happens to hold, and it is the one people wrongly treat
as an identity. Store acronyms or Allen ids; derive the index when you need it.

Most functions that take a region accept the Allen id. Converting runs through the arrays
directly:

```python
import numpy as np

i = int(np.flatnonzero(br.acronym == 'MOp')[0])   # acronym -> index
br.id[i]                                          # index   -> Allen id
```

## Left hemisphere regions have negative ids

The object holds **2655** entries: one `void` entry with id `0`, then **1327** right-hemisphere
regions with positive ids, then the same 1327 regions again for the left hemisphere with the
**same acronym and the negated id**.

```python
br.n_lr          # 1327 — the number of regions per hemisphere
br.id[19]        #  985  -> MOp, right
br.id[19 + 1327] # -985  -> MOp, left
br.acronym[19] == br.acronym[19 + 1327]   # True
```

So the sign of an Allen id carries the hemisphere, and `MOp` alone does not tell you which side
of the brain you are on. Two consequences:

- **Taking the absolute value merges hemispheres.** That is sometimes what you want and
  sometimes a silent bug; it is never the default you should assume.
- **A left-hemisphere region cannot be looked up by a positive id.** If your own data records
  hemisphere separately, apply the sign before joining, or the left side will land on the
  right.

The left index is always the right index plus `br.n_lr`, which is the cheapest way to move
between the two.

## Where this shows up next

The hierarchy is the machinery the mappings are built on, and the negative-id convention is
what makes two-hemisphere plotting work — see
[Brain region mappings](brain-region-mappings.qmd).
